passages.passage_text:
Until the early nineteenth century, orchestras in Europe commonly played without anyone standing in front of them. Time was kept by the concertmaster, who nodded or swept a bow from the first desk, or by a keyboardist who played continuo and signaled changes of pace with the hands. The ensemble worked because its members shared a repertoire, a style, and often a town. A symphony was usually new, performed once or twice, and rehearsed little; the players' task was to stay together, not to interpret. When a dedicated beater of time did appear, contemporaries were not sure what to make of him. Some thought him a kind of human metronome, and in the opera house he was sometimes nearly that: Jean-Baptiste Lully, in 1687, is said to have marked the beat by pounding the floor with a heavy staff, and to have died after the staff pierced his foot.

The standard account treats the conductor's rise as a response to scores that had outgrown the old methods. Orchestras expanded, harmony grew more adventurous, and rhythms began to shift in ways that a violinist's nod could not manage. There is truth in this. But it explains the conductor's necessity better than his authority. A time-beater needs no particular genius, and the nineteenth century soon decided that its conductors had a great deal. By mid-century the figure on the podium was credited with something beyond coordination: the power to reveal what a composition meant. Wagner argued that the conductor must grasp the melos of a work, its inner line of feeling, and then impose it on the players by sheer presence; tempo, in his view, was not a number but an expressive decision that changed from phrase to phrase. Berlioz, who led his own enormous works, wrote a treatise on the art, and Hans von Bulow made a career of standing for scrupulous fidelity to what he took to be the composer's intentions.

These two ideals, the interpreter who discloses a work's spirit and the servant who obeys its letter, were rarely compatible, and the tension has never been resolved. It sharpened in the twentieth century, when recording allowed a conductor's decisions to be compared across decades. Listeners discovered that the same symphony could last forty minutes under one baton and fifty under another, and that each performance claimed to be the authentic one. Toscanini was praised for severity toward the score, yet his readings were as personal as anyone's, his famous literalism consisting largely of a particular and rigorously maintained view of the music. Furtwangler, by contrast, was admired for a flexibility so extreme that critics wondered whether the composer still had a say.

It would be tempting to conclude that the conductor's authority is therefore an illusion, an inflated claim propped up by ceremony. Yet this overlooks a quieter fact about what a conductor actually does. Much of his influence is exerted through ordinary choices: which passage to repeat in rehearsal, which player to single out, how long to wait before the downbeat. These are small decisions, but in an ensemble of eighty people with no other center of judgment, they accumulate into a recognizable sound. The conductor's power, on this view, is neither the mystical access to the composer's mind that Wagner claimed nor the empty pomp his skeptics allege. It is the power of a person whom many others have agreed, for practical reasons, to follow, and the agreement is what makes the rest possible. Interpretation emerges from this arrangement rather than preceding it.

questions.stem: Which of the following best expresses the main idea of the passage?

options.A: The conductor arose because modern scores grew too complex for a concertmaster's nod to coordinate the players.
options.B: Recordings have shown that conductors who claim fidelity to a score are merely imposing personal taste upon it, so that the claim of fidelity is only a pose adopted to impress audiences.
options.C: The conductor's authority, though defended by rival ideals of interpretation, rests mainly on a practical agreement among players to follow one person.
options.D: The belief that a conductor can reveal a composer's meaning has been refuted by differences in performance length.

questions.explanation: Correct: C) The final paragraph concludes that authority arises from the arrangement of players and conductor, after the second and third paragraphs show that neither ideal of interpretation can ground it. Why the others are wrong: A) This is the standard account, which the author qualifies as explaining necessity but not authority. B) Recordings exposed the tension between ideals, but the author does not reduce all fidelity to personal taste, and the passage ends elsewhere. D) The author calls the mystical claim overstated but never says differences in length refute it, and the main point concerns the source of authority.
questions.trap: Picking the standard historical account because it opens the passage, rather than the author's own thesis at the end.

questions.stem: The author most likely mentions Lully's staff in order to:

options.A: demonstrate that conductors were dangerous colleagues because of the crude implements they used to command orchestras.
options.B: support the claim that the first conductors were admired for expressive interpretation rather than for keeping time.
options.C: show that the earliest time-beaters were humble figures.
options.D: illustrate that opera orchestras were more disciplined than concert orchestras in the period before the nineteenth century.

questions.explanation: Correct: C) The anecdote shows a beater of time pounding the floor, supporting the point that early leaders merely marked the pulse. Why the others are wrong: A) The injury is incidental; the author is not making a point about danger to players. B) The anecdote concerns pounding out the beat, which is the opposite of interpretation. D) Nothing in the passage compares the discipline of opera and concert orchestras.
questions.trap: Treating a vivid detail as evidence for a claim the passage never makes, such as danger or discipline.

questions.stem: The author's statement that the standard account "explains the conductor's necessity better than his authority" most nearly means that:

options.A: growing complexity shows why someone had to coordinate the players, but not why that person came to be seen as the revealer of a work's meaning.
options.B: complex scores made conductors indispensable, but players resented the power that this indispensability gave them.
options.C: the standard account misdates the point at which orchestras grew large and their harmonies more adventurous.
options.D: the need for coordination was real but was in practice met by the concertmaster instead of a separate conductor.

questions.explanation: Correct: A) The next sentences contrast a time-beater needing no genius with nineteenth-century credit given to the conductor's insight. Why the others are wrong: B) Player resentment is never mentioned. C) The author accepts the account's facts and says there is truth in it. D) The concertmaster served in the earlier period; the passage says the conductor later became the coordinator.
questions.trap: Reading a claim about explanatory scope as a claim that the facts are wrong.

questions.stem: Which of the following is most consistent with the passage's description of Toscanini?

options.A: His readings were looser than Furtwangler's, whom critics regarded as severe toward the score.
options.B: His claim to literal fidelity itself reflected a personal conception of the work.
options.C: His performances were indistinguishable in length and character from those of his contemporaries.
options.D: He rejected the view that a conductor should serve the composer's intentions in favor of freely expressive readings.

questions.explanation: Correct: B) The passage says his literalism consisted largely of a particular and rigorously maintained view of the music. Why the others are wrong: A) The passage reverses these reputations: Toscanini was severe and Furtwangler flexible. C) The passage says only that performances of the same symphony varied widely in length. D) He was praised for severity toward the score, so he did not reject fidelity.
questions.trap: Assuming that a reputation for literalism means the performances were impersonal.

questions.stem: Which of the following findings would most undermine the author's account of how conductors exert their influence?

options.A: Audiences rate concerts more highly when they can see the conductor than when they cannot.
options.B: Conductors who rehearse for longer periods produce performances that critics judge more faithful to the score.
options.C: In recorded rehearsals of large orchestras, players disregard the conductor's choices about repetition and timing and follow the concertmaster instead.
options.D: Recordings of one symphony by different conductors differ in length by as much as ten minutes.

questions.explanation: Correct: C) If players ignore these ordinary choices, the accumulation of small decisions into a recognizable sound is no longer explained. Why the others are wrong: A) Audience ratings say nothing about how influence is exerted in rehearsal. B) This concerns fidelity, and could be consistent with influence through rehearsal choices. D) Differences in length are consistent with the author's account of conductors' choices.
questions.trap: Choosing evidence about audiences or critics when the claim concerns influence inside the orchestra.

questions.stem: The authority of the conductor described in the final paragraph is most like the authority of:

options.A: a monarch who claims the right to rule through divine appointment and personal access to a higher truth.
options.B: a referee who enforces rules written by an outside body and has no discretion in applying them.
options.C: a team captain whose standing rests on teammates' agreement and on many small decisions.
options.D: a timekeeper whose only task is to signal the end of each interval and who exercises no judgment.

questions.explanation: Correct: C) Both depend on voluntary agreement to follow and on accumulated routine choices. Why the others are wrong: A) This resembles Wagner's mystical claim, which the author rejects. B) This resembles the servant who obeys the letter and is not based on consent. D) This resembles the early time-beater, whom the author contrasts with the later conductor.
questions.trap: Matching the analogy to the most dramatic image of authority rather than the one the author endorses.

passages.passage_text:
In the industrial towns of northern England in the nineteenth century, a mill or colliery of any size was likely to have a brass band. Employers bought the instruments, paid for the uniforms, and hired a professional teacher; in return the band carried the firm's name to festivals and contests, and its members, who were drawn from the workforce, were expected to embody the habits an employer prized: punctuality, sobriety, and discipline. Historians who read these arrangements as paternalism have a strong case. The band was an advertisement, a means of binding skilled workers to the firm, and an alternative to the public house, which employers regarded as the chief enemy of a reliable labor force.

The difficulty is that the same evidence supports a very different story. Valved brass instruments became cheap through mass production in the middle of the century, and players did not need to read music fluently to join, because teachers drilled parts by ear and by rote. A man who could not afford a piano or a violin could belong to a band for a few shillings a week. Rehearsals took place several evenings a week, and the players, not the owners, decided who was good enough to sit in the front row. The contest movement, which grew around annual competitions near Manchester from the 1850s, rewarded precision and musical ambition, and bands began to compete by hiring famous conductors, commissioning arrangements of operatic and choral works, and traveling by railway to meet rivals. Some historians therefore describe the bands as an expression of working-class pride, a cultural world that workers built for themselves with borrowed money.

Neither description survives contact with the details of particular bands. Employers who sponsored bands often discovered that sponsorship did not purchase loyalty. During strikes, bands sometimes played on the picket line or refused to perform at the owner's gala, and a band whose firm failed could simply change its name and carry on under a new patron, its instruments and repertoire intact. Conversely, bands that began as the independent projects of a chapel or a neighborhood frequently accepted gifts from local manufacturers, since uniforms and professional tuition were costly and the contest circuit was unforgiving to the poor. The supposed contrast between control from above and expression from below depends on picturing the band as a single object with a single function. In practice it was a bundle of resources: instruments, rehearsal space, status, a calendar of public appearances.

The same resource could serve different interests at different times. A patron who funded a band acquired a visible symbol of his generosity, but he also gave the players an organization, a treasury, and a public voice that they could use as they wished. What patrons could not control was the musical standard itself. Because contests were judged by outsiders, a band's reputation depended on its quality, not on its owner's wishes, and ambitious players soon discovered that excellence gave them bargaining power. A sponsor who withdrew support risked losing a famous band to a rival firm. The bands thus illustrate a more general feature of cultural patronage: money can create an institution, but once the institution has its own measures of success, those who paid for it may find that they have bought something they only partly own.

questions.stem: Which of the following best summarizes the author's view of nineteenth-century brass bands?

options.A: They resist classification as either employer control or worker self-expression, since patronage produced resources that served several interests.
options.B: They were mainly instruments of employer paternalism, since sponsors supplied instruments, uniforms, and teachers and in return expected punctuality, sobriety, and deference from every player.
options.C: They were independent working-class creations that employers tried and failed to take over.
options.D: They were transformed by the contest movement into professional organizations responsive only to outside judges.

questions.explanation: Correct: A) The author argues the supposed contrast depends on picturing the band as having a single function. Why the others are wrong: B) This is one reading the author accepts only in part and then challenges. C) The author notes that independent bands also accepted gifts from manufacturers. D) The judges set the standard, but the author does not say bands answered only to them.
questions.trap: Choosing one of the two competing historical readings instead of the author's rejection of the contrast.

questions.stem: According to the passage, a worker of modest means could join a band because:

options.A: employers gave free instruments to any employee willing to rehearse several evenings every week.
options.B: instruments were cheap and parts could be learned by ear.
options.C: contest organizers subsidized fees for players from firms that could not afford professional teachers.
options.D: bands admitted only those who already read music well, which kept the cost of instruction low.

questions.explanation: Correct: B) The passage says valved brass instruments became cheap and teachers drilled parts by ear and rote. Why the others are wrong: A) The passage says employers bought instruments for the band but not that any employee received one free. C) Contest subsidies are not mentioned. D) The passage says players did not need to read music fluently.
questions.trap: Picking a plausible-sounding subsidy that the passage never mentions.

questions.stem: The author mentions bands that played on picket lines or changed patrons in order to show that:

options.A: brass bands were political organizations seeking the overthrow of the factory system.
options.B: the contest circuit forced bands to move constantly from one firm to another.
options.C: employers consistently underestimated the cost of maintaining a band.
options.D: sponsorship did not buy the loyalty that employers expected.

questions.explanation: Correct: D) These episodes are offered as evidence that employers' investment did not secure deference. Why the others are wrong: A) Playing on a picket line shows sympathy with strikers, not a revolutionary program. B) Changing patrons is mentioned as a survival tactic when a firm failed, not as a constant pattern. C) Cost is raised later in connection with poor bands, not here.
questions.trap: Taking a single illustration as a statement of a broader political claim.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that the "social control" reading and the "working-class expression" reading share which assumption?

options.A: That the contest movement was the most important force shaping band life.
options.B: That employers had no reason to sponsor bands.
options.C: That bands were found only in mining communities.
options.D: That a band can be understood in terms of one function serving a single group.

questions.explanation: Correct: D) The author says the contrast depends on picturing the band as a single object with a single function. Why the others are wrong: A) Contests are discussed in only one reading. B) The first reading depends on employers having reasons. C) Mills and collieries are both mentioned, and no such assumption is attributed.
questions.trap: Selecting a detail that appears in one reading instead of the premise common to both.

questions.stem: Which of the following observations would most strengthen the author's concluding claim about cultural patronage?

options.A: A sponsored orchestra, judged by outside critics, uses its fame to bargain with its sponsor.
options.B: A museum donor requires that a collection be displayed under the donor's name for fifty years.
options.C: A company choir disbands as soon as the firm withdraws the funding that sustained it.
options.D: A foundation's scholars produce work that earns public praise for the donor who financed the project.

questions.explanation: Correct: A) This mirrors bands whose outside-judged excellence gave them bargaining power over patrons. Why the others are wrong: B) This shows a donor exercising control, which does not support the claim. C) This shows dependence, the opposite of the partial independence the author describes. D) This shows patronage serving the patron, with no loss of control.
questions.trap: Choosing an example of patronage in general rather than one in which the patron loses control.

questions.stem: Which finding would most weaken the author's claim that outside judging gave players bargaining power?

options.A: Bands that won contests received larger gifts from local manufacturers than bands that did not, and the largest gifts tended to go to bands led by the most famous conductors.
options.B: Judges at contests were drawn from outside the band's own town and firm.
options.C: Many players practiced several evenings per week, sometimes after long shifts in the mill.
options.D: Rival firms showed no interest in hiring away famous bands, and sponsors who withdrew support suffered no loss of prestige.

questions.explanation: Correct: D) If rivals did not want the bands and withdrawal cost nothing, excellence would not translate into leverage. Why the others are wrong: A) This suggests that excellence was rewarded, consistent with leverage. B) The claim already assumes judges were outsiders. C) The effort of players is irrelevant to bargaining power.
questions.trap: Choosing a finding that restates the premise instead of cutting the link from excellence to leverage.

passages.passage_text:
In the 1770s the French philosopher Denis Diderot wrote a dialogue on acting that overturned what most theatergoers believed. The audience, he observed, wants to think that a great performer is carried away by feeling, weeping real tears over the death of a fictional daughter. Diderot argued the opposite. The actor who is swept up in emotion is at the mercy of mood, health, and the weather; he is magnificent on Tuesday and wooden on Thursday. The truly great actor, by contrast, feels little during the performance and produces the same sublime effect every night, because he has studied the outward signs of passion, rehearsed them until they are exact, and deploys them with a cool and observant mind. Sensibility, in other words, is the mark of the mediocre; the great performer's gift is judgment.

The thesis, which Diderot called a paradox, was not published until well after his death, but it has shaped every later argument about the craft. In the early twentieth century Konstantin Stanislavski built a method of training that appeared to say the reverse: the actor should draw on memories of his own experience in order to bring real feeling to the stage, so that the character's grief is rooted in something the performer has known. Bertolt Brecht, in turn, objected to both traditions. He wanted the audience to be kept at a critical distance from the story, and he asked his actors to demonstrate a character rather than become one, so that spectators would think about social conditions rather than weep over fate. Each school claims a theory of what actors really do, and each is supported by testimony from celebrated performers.

That testimony, however, is the weak point. Actors who report on their own states during a performance are asked to observe an activity while performing it, and the evidence of psychology suggests that such reports are poor guides to what is actually happening. Some performers who swear they feel nothing show racing hearts and tears; others who describe total absorption are plainly in command of timing and voice down to the second. Indeed the most common report from experienced actors is that both are true at once: they are moved, and they are watching themselves be moved, and they adjust their weeping to the size of the theater. If so, the opposition between feeling and control may be an artifact of the way the question was framed.

What the quarrel really concerns, I would argue, is a question about value rather than a question about fact. To prefer Diderot's actor is to prize craft: the reliable production of an effect, admirable in the way a violinist's technique is admirable. To prefer Stanislavski's is to prize authenticity: the sense that a human being is truly present before us, taking a risk. These are different goods, and a performance can have one without the other. An audience that is moved by a flawless demonstration of grief has been given something real, and an audience that watches a tearful but clumsy performance has been given something real too. Asking what is going on inside the actor will not tell us which good to value more, and the persistence of the debate for two and a half centuries suggests that nothing could.

questions.stem: The main point of the passage is that the dispute over whether actors feel or control emotion:

options.A: shows that Diderot was correct that great actors feel nothing, and that later schools have only obscured his insight.
options.B: has been settled by psychology in favor of Stanislavski's method of drawing on personal memory.
options.C: can be settled by what experienced performers report about themselves.
options.D: is better read as a disagreement about whether craft or authenticity is more valuable.

questions.explanation: Correct: D) The final paragraph recasts the quarrel as one about value rather than fact. Why the others are wrong: A) The author doubts any account of the actor's inner state can be established. B) Psychology is cited only to cast doubt on introspective reports. C) The author calls such testimony the weak point of the debate.
questions.trap: Picking an option that sounds like a resolution when the author argues that none is available.

questions.stem: According to Diderot, the actor swept up by emotion performs poorly because:

options.A: he lacks the sensibility needed to understand the suffering of the character he plays.
options.B: he studies the outward signs of passion too closely to produce a spontaneous effect.
options.C: the quality of his work varies with his moods.
options.D: he fails to keep the attention of an audience that wants real tears from a performer.

questions.explanation: Correct: C) Diderot says he is magnificent one night and wooden the next, at the mercy of mood, health, and weather. Why the others are wrong: A) Diderot treats sensibility as the mark of the mediocre, not as a lack. B) This is the habit of the great actor in Diderot's view. D) Diderot says audiences want real tears, but this is not why the swept-up actor is weak.
questions.trap: Confusing the traits Diderot attributes to the great actor with those of the mediocre one.

questions.stem: The author regards the testimony of celebrated performers about their stage experience as:

options.A: decisive evidence for Stanislavski's view over Diderot's.
options.B: unreliable evidence, since people are poor observers of their own states while they are performing.
options.C: flawed evidence because performers conceal their methods from rival actors.
options.D: valuable evidence that is biased toward Brecht's view.

questions.explanation: Correct: B) The third paragraph calls it the weak point and cites psychology showing such reports are poor guides. Why the others are wrong: A) The author says each school is backed by testimony and therefore none is decisive. C) Concealment is never raised. D) Brecht's view is described only as an objection to both traditions.
questions.trap: Treating the testimony the schools rely on as dependable because of its vividness.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the most reasonable inference about Brecht's view of acting?

options.A: He agreed with Diderot that actors should feel nothing and with Stanislavski that audiences should weep.
options.B: He believed that audiences cannot be moved by performances that demonstrate rather than embody a character, and he therefore urged actors to embody their roles more fully.
options.C: He thought actors should draw on personal memories so that the audience is distanced from the story.
options.D: He considered emotional absorption in a character an obstacle to the social understanding he wanted theater to produce.

questions.explanation: Correct: D) Brecht wanted critical distance so that spectators think about social conditions instead of weeping. Why the others are wrong: A) The passage says he objected to both traditions. B) His aim was critical thought, not emotional response, so he had no such belief. C) Drawing on memory is Stanislavski's method, and it is not tied to distancing.
questions.trap: Mixing the three schools' positions together and attributing parts of one to another.

questions.stem: Suppose actors who report strong emotion on stage and actors who report none produce performances that audiences rate as equally moving. The author would most likely take this to show that:

options.A: Stanislavski's method is more effective than Diderot's for producing emotion in an audience.
options.B: great actors must feel nothing in order to keep their performances steady from night to night.
options.C: audiences are unable to distinguish genuine feeling from demonstrated feeling under any circumstances.
options.D: reports of an actor's inner state are a poor guide to the effect produced.

questions.explanation: Correct: D) This fits the author's claim that asking what goes on inside actors will not settle the question. Why the others are wrong: A) Equal ratings give no advantage to either method. B) Equal ratings do not show that feeling harms steadiness. C) The finding concerns two particular groups and cannot establish an inability under all circumstances.
questions.trap: Overgeneralizing a single finding into a sweeping claim about all audiences or all actors.

questions.stem: Which of the following disputes is most similar to the one the author describes in the final paragraph?

options.A: A dispute over whether a bridge failed from corrosion or overload, which engineers can settle by inspecting the wreckage.
options.B: A disagreement about a pianist's age, which can be settled by consulting birth records.
options.C: A debate about whether a pianist should be judged on flawless technique or on risk-taking spirit, which no study of the pianist's nerves could settle.
options.D: A quarrel over which of two pianists practiced longer, which their diaries could resolve.

questions.explanation: Correct: C) Like the acting debate, it turns on which good to value, so facts about inner states cannot decide it. Why the others are wrong: A) This is a factual dispute settled by evidence. B) This is also factual. D) This is factual and resolvable with records.
questions.trap: Choosing the example that merely involves performers rather than the one that shares the dispute's structure.

passages.passage_text:
A familiar story about astronomy holds that for fourteen centuries Europeans clung to a clumsy theory in which the planets rode on wheels upon wheels, until Copernicus swept the clutter away by placing the sun at the center. The story makes the Ptolemaic system a monument to stubbornness and the Copernican a triumph of simplicity. It is neat, and it is wrong in almost every particular.

Consider first what the Ptolemaic system was for. Its purpose was to predict where each planet would appear against the stars, and by that standard it was remarkably good. Using circles whose centers could be shifted and smaller circles, or epicycles, carried along larger ones, astronomers could calculate positions accurately enough to compile almanacs, fix the date of Easter, and guide navigators. A theory that worked so well for so long was not an obvious candidate for abandonment. The device of the epicycle was also not an ad hoc patch. It was a flexible mathematical tool that, like a Fourier series, could represent almost any periodic motion to whatever accuracy one demanded, which is exactly why its failures were hard to detect.

Nor did Copernicus's system win by being simpler or more accurate. Committed to the ancient principle that celestial motions must be uniform and circular, Copernicus kept circles, and to match the observations he needed epicycles of his own; his system contained about as many circles as his predecessors', and in its first versions it predicted positions no better than theirs. What it offered was of a different kind. In the Ptolemaic scheme, the backward loops of the planets required a separate epicycle for each planet, whose size had to be fixed by observation, and nothing in the theory explained why the loops of Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn always occurred when those planets were opposite the sun. In the Copernican scheme the loops arose automatically from the earth's own motion, and the order of the planets and the relative sizes of their orbits followed from the observations without further assumptions. This was an advance in explanation: one hypothesis accounting for facts that the older theory had to treat as unrelated coincidences.

The advance was not decisive, because explanation had to be weighed against other commitments. A moving earth contradicted the physics of the day, in which heavy bodies fell toward the center of the universe and a spinning earth should have flung loose objects into the sky. Anyone who judged theories by their consistency with accepted physics could reasonably prefer the older system. Only gradually did the balance shift. Tycho Brahe's precise observations, Kepler's discovery that planetary orbits are ellipses, Galileo's telescope observations, and finally a physics of inertia and gravitation, which made the earth's motion intelligible, together turned a controversial hypothesis into settled knowledge.

The moral is not that the old theory was secretly as good as the new. It is that theory choice rarely pits a bad theory against a good one. It weighs several virtues, among them accuracy, explanatory unity, and harmony with the rest of what is known, which seldom point in the same direction at the same time. Historians who judge past scientists by the outcome alone mistake the end of an argument for its beginning.

questions.stem: Which of the following best states the main idea of the passage?

options.A: The shift from Ptolemaic to Copernican astronomy involved competing theoretical virtues, not a contest between a bad theory and a good one.
options.B: The Ptolemaic system lasted because astronomers deferred to ancient authority despite its obvious complexity, and it was abandoned as soon as simpler alternatives were proposed.
options.C: Copernicus's system prevailed because it used fewer circles and predicted planetary positions more accurately.
options.D: Kepler's ellipses and Galileo's telescope observations were sufficient to establish the motion of the earth.

questions.explanation: Correct: A) The closing paragraph says theory choice weighs several virtues that seldom point in the same direction. Why the others are wrong: B) The author argues the system was predictively successful, not merely authoritative. C) The passage says it had about as many circles and was no more accurate at first. D) The passage says a physics of inertia and gravitation was also needed.
questions.trap: Accepting the familiar story the passage sets out to correct.

questions.stem: According to the passage, what initial advantage did the Copernican system have over the Ptolemaic system?

options.A: It predicted the positions of the planets more precisely than the Ptolemaic system could.
options.B: It explained retrograde loops and planetary order without extra assumptions.
options.C: It dispensed with epicycles by substituting elliptical orbits for circles.
options.D: It agreed more closely with the accepted physics of falling bodies and a stationary center.

questions.explanation: Correct: B) The passage says loops arose from the earth's motion and the order of planets followed from observation. Why the others are wrong: A) The passage says its first versions were no better in prediction. C) Ellipses came from Kepler, after Copernicus. D) The passage says a moving earth contradicted the physics of the day.
questions.trap: Crediting Copernicus with Kepler's later improvements or with an accuracy advantage he lacked.

questions.stem: The comparison of the epicycle to a Fourier series suggests that epicycles:

options.A: could be adjusted to fit almost any periodic motion, which concealed their shortcomings.
options.B: were mathematically unsound and survived only because of tradition.
options.C: were introduced by Ptolemy to correct specific failures in earlier theories, and were added one at a time to rescue the system from refutation.
options.D: were an unsophisticated device soon replaced by more precise methods.

questions.explanation: Correct: A) The author says this flexibility is why its failures were hard to detect. Why the others are wrong: B) The author calls them a flexible tool, not an unsound one. C) Origins are not discussed. D) The author describes epicycles as lasting a very long time and being sophisticated.
questions.trap: Reading a mathematical analogy as a criticism of the device.

questions.stem: Which of the following does the author cite as a reason a reasonable astronomer might have preferred the Ptolemaic system?

options.A: The Copernican system could not account for the backward loops of the planets.
options.B: A moving earth conflicted with prevailing physics, in which heavy bodies fell toward the center of the universe.
options.C: Tycho Brahe's observations contradicted the order of the planets proposed by Copernicus.
options.D: Epicycles gave more accurate predictions than ellipses.

questions.explanation: Correct: B) The fourth paragraph states this directly. Why the others are wrong: A) The Copernican system explained them automatically. C) Brahe's observations are cited as helping the eventual shift. D) The passage does not compare epicycles with ellipses in accuracy.
questions.trap: Confusing evidence that eventually favored Copernicus with reasons for resistance to it.

questions.stem: Which of the following situations best parallels that of an astronomer considering Copernicus's system in the early sixteenth century?

options.A: A mathematician who drops a method after learning it gives wrong answers to standard problems.
options.B: A physician weighing a model of disease that explains many symptoms by one cause but predicts no better and clashes with accepted chemistry.
options.C: An engineer who keeps an old design even though a new one proves cheaper and safer in every test, so that the choice involves no real tradeoff at all.
options.D: A historian who accepts a theory because it was proposed by the most famous scholar of his time.

questions.explanation: Correct: B) Like Copernicus, the new model gains explanatory unity but lacks predictive advantage and conflicts with other accepted knowledge. Why the others are wrong: A) This involves a clear failure and no conflicting virtues. C) The new option wins on every measure, so there is no tradeoff. D) This turns on authority, not on weighing theoretical virtues.
questions.trap: Choosing a case with a plain winner when the parallel requires conflicting virtues.

questions.stem: Which finding would most undermine the author's claim about early Copernican predictions?

options.A: Copernicus's system contained about as many circles as Ptolemy's when all epicycles were counted.
options.B: Navigators using Ptolemaic tables rarely lost their way on sea voyages in the same period.
options.C: Almanacs based on Copernicus's tables proved clearly more accurate than Ptolemaic ones.
options.D: Most astronomers who studied the Copernican system after its publication rejected its claim of a moving earth.

questions.explanation: Correct: C) This directly contradicts the claim that early predictions were no better. Why the others are wrong: A) This agrees with the passage. B) This is consistent with the Ptolemaic system's practical accuracy. D) This concerns acceptance and does not bear on accuracy.
questions.trap: Selecting evidence about acceptance or practice instead of evidence about predictive accuracy.

passages.passage_text:
It has often been said that science owes more to the steam engine than the steam engine owes to science. The remark is an exaggeration, but it points at an inconvenient fact for anyone who pictures technology as applied science, a process in which discoveries made in laboratories are carried out into the world and turned into machines. The sequence in the case of steam runs the other way. Thomas Newcomen's atmospheric engine was pumping water out of English mines in 1712, and James Watt's improvement, the separate condenser, came in the 1760s, some sixty years before anyone produced a satisfactory theory of how heat produces motive power. The engineers who built these machines worked by trial, by craft knowledge, and by careful measurement of what made one engine burn less coal than another.

When theory arrived, it arrived in response to the machines. In 1824 the French engineer Sadi Carnot published a short book asking a question no one had posed: is there a limit to the work that can be obtained from a given quantity of heat, and does it depend on the working substance, whether steam, air, or alcohol? He argued that the maximum depends only on the temperatures between which the engine operates, and he reached this conclusion by comparing the engine to a waterwheel, in which the power obtained depends on the height through which water falls. The analogy rested on the caloric theory, according to which heat was a fluid conserved in the process, and that theory was soon discredited. Yet Carnot's central result survived. When Clausius and Kelvin, in the following decades, reconciled his argument with the conservation of energy, they produced the first and second laws of thermodynamics, in which a limit on efficiency is a consequence of the nature of heat itself.

It would be as mistaken to reverse the old story as to retain it. The engine did not simply give birth to a theory that then sat idly in textbooks. Thermodynamics fed back into engineering, though more slowly than legend suggests. It supplied designers with a measure against which any engine could be judged, and it showed which improvements were worth pursuing and which, like the search for a better working fluid, were not. Engineers such as Rankine adapted the theory to steam practice, and later developments, such as compound expansion and the steam turbine, drew on it to set targets. The steam engine had also supplied science with something more than a puzzle. The indicator diagram, a device invented to monitor the performance of engines, gave physicists a way of plotting pressure against volume that became an indispensable tool of thermodynamics itself.

A more accurate picture, then, is of two traditions with separate origins that gradually learned to use each other's products. Craftsmen produced working devices and instruments; natural philosophers produced concepts and principles that explained, constrained, and sometimes redirected the devices. Neither tradition was subordinate to the other. The lesson for the present is that policies which assume innovation flows only from basic research to application misread the history, and that those which dismiss theory as a luxury misread it as badly.

questions.stem: Which of the following best expresses the central claim of the passage?

options.A: Thermodynamics arose entirely from the study of steam engines and had little effect on later engineering.
options.B: Carnot's reliance on caloric theory was so flawed that his conclusions on engine efficiency had no lasting value for later engineers or physicists, who started over.
options.C: Technology and science developed through mutual influence, with the steam engine preceding thermodynamic theory and later being guided by it.
options.D: Technology depends on basic research, since engines improved only after theories of heat were developed.

questions.explanation: Correct: C) The final paragraph describes two traditions that learned to use each other's products. Why the others are wrong: A) The passage describes thermodynamic theory feeding back into engineering. B) The passage says his central result survived. D) The engine preceded theory by decades.
questions.trap: Preferring a one-directional story even though the passage rejects both directions.

questions.stem: The author mentions the indicator diagram in order to show that:

options.A: Watt's separate condenser was based on an understanding of the theory of heat.
options.B: engineering practice supplied science with a useful tool.
options.C: Rankine adapted thermodynamic principles to the design of steam turbines.
options.D: experimental instruments are more valuable to physics than are theoretical principles.

questions.explanation: Correct: B) The diagram was invented to monitor engines and became a tool of thermodynamics. Why the others are wrong: A) The passage says the condenser preceded theory by decades. C) Rankine is mentioned elsewhere and the diagram is not linked to him. D) The author makes no such ranking.
questions.trap: Linking the diagram to the theory-to-practice direction instead of the practice-to-theory direction it illustrates.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that Carnot's central result survived the discrediting of the caloric theory because:

options.A: the caloric theory was later shown to be correct in the case of steam.
options.B: its claim that efficiency depends on temperatures could be reconciled with energy conservation once the caloric assumption was dropped.
options.C: Clausius and Kelvin had proposed the same result before Carnot published.
options.D: experiments on steam confirmed the waterwheel analogy that Carnot had used.

questions.explanation: Correct: B) Clausius and Kelvin reconciled his argument with conservation of energy, producing the laws of thermodynamics. Why the others are wrong: A) The passage says the theory was soon discredited. C) They came in the decades after Carnot. D) The analogy rested on caloric and is not said to have been confirmed.
questions.trap: Assuming a result survives only if the reasoning behind it was correct.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward the remark that science owes more to the steam engine than the engine owes to science is best described as:

options.A: approving: it states the true relation between science and technology, and the author endorses it as an accurate summary of the history.
options.B: dismissive: it is a slogan with no basis in the history of engines.
options.C: qualified: it overstates the case but points to a fact that the applied-science model ignores.
options.D: neutral: it is reported without evaluation as the view of historians.

questions.explanation: Correct: C) The author calls it an exaggeration that points at an inconvenient fact. Why the others are wrong: A) The author calls it an exaggeration and later rejects reversing the old story. B) The author grants that it points at an inconvenient fact. D) The author evaluates it directly in the first paragraph.
questions.trap: Reading a mild criticism as outright rejection or endorsement.

questions.stem: Which of the following findings would most weaken the author's claim that thermodynamics fed back into engineering?

options.A: Records show that the designers of compound engines and turbines were unaware of thermodynamic theory and worked entirely by trial and error.
options.B: Historians find that Rankine published widely on steam practice and corresponded with working engineers about the design of boilers, cylinders, and engine performance.
options.C: Carnot's book remained little known for a decade after it was published.
options.D: Watt's condenser reduced fuel consumption substantially compared with Newcomen's engine.

questions.explanation: Correct: A) This removes the channel through which theory is said to have guided later designs. Why the others are wrong: B) This supports the link. C) The delay does not show that later engineers failed to use the theory. D) This concerns the earlier period before theory.
questions.trap: Picking evidence about the early period when the claim concerns later feedback.

questions.stem: The author's discussion implies that a policy of funding only basic research, in the expectation that useful applications will follow, would be:

options.A: sound, because technology depends on theoretical discoveries made first in laboratories and only afterward carried out into machines.
options.B: sound, provided that the basic research is directed toward problems posed by industry.
options.C: mistaken, because theory has contributed little to the improvement of machines.
options.D: mistaken, because in the case of steam innovation came from practice to theory as well as the reverse.

questions.explanation: Correct: D) The author says policies assuming one-way flow from research to application misread history. Why the others are wrong: A) This is the applied-science model the author rejects. B) The author does not endorse any version of the one-way policy. C) The author says dismissing theory is as mistaken as ignoring practice.
questions.trap: Overcorrecting to the opposite extreme and rejecting theory altogether.

passages.passage_text:
According to a long tradition, Aristotle held that heavier bodies fall faster than light ones, and for centuries no one thought to doubt it. Galileo, in his Discourses on Two New Sciences, is reputed to have disposed of the view without dropping anything from a tower. Suppose, he said, that a heavy stone falls faster than a light one. Now tie the two together. The light stone, being slower, should hold back the heavy one, so that the combination falls more slowly than the heavy stone alone. But the combination is heavier than either stone, so it should fall faster than the heavy stone alone. The assumption therefore yields two incompatible predictions. Since both cannot be true, the assumption must be false, and the natural conclusion is that all bodies fall at the same rate.

What is striking about this argument is that it requires no new observations. Its conclusion concerns the physical world, yet it seems to have been reached from an armchair, and philosophers have found this puzzling. If experience is the only source of knowledge about nature, how can a mental exercise teach anything about it? One response is that thought experiments are a species of Platonic insight, in which the mind grasps the laws of nature directly, the way it grasps a mathematical truth. The opposing response is deflationary. On this view a thought experiment is simply an argument in picturesque dress. Its premises are things we already know from experience or assume as part of a theory, and its conclusion follows by ordinary logic, so that anything it teaches could have been taught by stating the premises and the inference in plain prose. The vividness of the scenario is a rhetorical flourish, and the appearance of a special route to knowledge an illusion.

The deflationary account has the advantage of sobriety, and it correctly observes that Galileo's argument can be set out as a logical derivation. But I think that it underestimates what the reconstruction leaves out. A reconstruction shows that the conclusion follows, and it does not show how anyone could have seen that it follows. The steps in Galileo's argument are not obvious until the two stones are imagined bound together, and the scenario does something that a list of premises cannot: it makes us notice that two commitments we held at once, that weight determines speed and that a compound body is the sum of its parts, cannot both be maintained. The value of the experiment lies in organizing what we already know in such a way that a hidden inconsistency becomes visible.

This is a modest power, but it is a real one. Thought experiments do not conjure facts out of nothing, so the Platonist claims too much. Neither are they mere decoration, so the deflationist claims too little. They resemble a well-drawn diagram in geometry: the diagram contains nothing that was not already implied by the axioms, yet without it the proof might never be found. And like a diagram, a thought experiment can mislead, since a vivid scenario may lead the imagination to supply assumptions that the reasoner has not noticed adding. The right attitude toward them is therefore the one we take toward other instruments of inquiry: appreciation of their usefulness, and vigilance about the ways they fail.

questions.stem: Which of the following best summarizes the author's view of thought experiments?

options.A: They show that conclusions about nature can sometimes be reached without any experience of the world, so that pure thought can replace observation in science.
options.B: They can be reduced to logical arguments, so their vivid scenarios serve only rhetorical purposes.
options.C: They are unreliable because they can mislead, so scientists should depend on observation alone.
options.D: They are neither a mysterious source of knowledge nor mere rhetoric but tools that expose inconsistencies among beliefs already held.

questions.explanation: Correct: D) The fourth paragraph says they do not conjure facts and are not decoration. Why the others are wrong: A) The author says the premises come from prior experience. B) This is the deflationary view the author finds too limited. C) The author warns about misleading but still values them.
questions.trap: Choosing one of the two views the author rejects as too strong or too weak.

questions.stem: The comparison to a geometric diagram suggests that a thought experiment:

options.A: adds no new content but may make a proof discoverable.
options.B: provides evidence that independent reasoning cannot supply, and so substitutes for the axioms.
options.C: is more reliable than a verbal argument because it rests on visual perception.
options.D: is mere decoration that can be removed with no loss because the proof is already complete.

questions.explanation: Correct: A) The diagram contains nothing not already implied by the axioms, yet the proof might never be found without it. Why the others are wrong: B) This overstates the role of the diagram. C) Reliability is not claimed, and the author notes diagrams can mislead. D) The author denies they are mere decoration.
questions.trap: Taking the phrase 'adds nothing new' to mean that it is useless.

questions.stem: In Galileo's argument, the combination of the two stones is first predicted to fall more slowly because:

options.A: the combined object is lighter than the heavy stone alone.
options.B: air resistance acts more strongly on bound objects than on single objects of the same total weight.
options.C: the slower light stone would be expected to hold back the faster heavy stone.
options.D: tying the stones together reduces the weight of each.

questions.explanation: Correct: C) The passage states this directly. Why the others are wrong: A) The combination is heavier, which is used for the second prediction. B) Air resistance is not mentioned. D) Weight is not changed by tying.
questions.trap: Confusing the first prediction with the second, which relies on the combined weight.

questions.stem: The author would most likely say that the weakness of the deflationary account is that it:

options.A: shows that a conclusion follows but not how anyone could have noticed that it does.
options.B: denies that Galileo's argument can be set out as a logical derivation.
options.C: holds that thought experiments give direct insight into nature's laws.
options.D: ignores that the premises of thought experiments must come from experience.

questions.explanation: Correct: A) The author says a reconstruction shows the conclusion follows but not how one could have seen that. Why the others are wrong: B) The author grants that it can be. C) That is the Platonist view. D) The deflationist emphasizes this point.
questions.trap: Attributing the Platonist position to the deflationist.

questions.stem: Suppose a thought experiment leads to a conclusion later contradicted by careful observation. The author would most likely say that:

options.A: thought experiments were never a legitimate instrument of scientific inquiry.
options.B: the contradiction proves that the premises were never based on any prior experience of the world.
options.C: Platonic insight is fallible, so thought experiments cannot reveal anything about the laws of nature.
options.D: the scenario probably led the imagination to supply an unnoticed assumption.

questions.explanation: Correct: D) The author warns that vivid scenarios can lead the imagination to add assumptions. Why the others are wrong: A) The author says they are useful and should be used with vigilance. B) A false conclusion does not show that the premises lacked experiential basis. C) The author does not hold the Platonic view, and fallibility does not imply uselessness.
questions.trap: Treating one failure as proof that the whole method is worthless.

questions.stem: Which of the following is most analogous to the way the author says a thought experiment works?

options.A: A chemist discovers a new element by heating an unknown ore.
options.B: A mathematician accepts a theorem on faith because of its elegance.
options.C: A mathematician accepts a theorem on faith because of its elegance and never examines the argument that is supposed to support it.
options.D: A lawyer arranges familiar facts in a sequence that makes the contradiction in a witness's testimony visible.

questions.explanation: Correct: D) Both reorganize what is already known so that a hidden inconsistency becomes visible. Why the others are wrong: A) This produces new facts through experiment. B) This is neither reorganization nor reasoning. C) This produces new content for enjoyment, not an exposure of inconsistency.
questions.trap: Choosing an example about discovery in general rather than the exposure of inconsistency.

passages.passage_text:
Most legal systems limit the time within which a lawsuit or prosecution may be brought. Wait too long to sue over a broken contract, and the claim is barred, whatever its merit. The rule can look perverse. A wrong does not become less wrong because years have passed, and a court that refuses to hear a legitimate grievance for the sake of a calendar seems to put administrative convenience above justice. Yet statutes of limitations are among the oldest and most widespread features of law, which suggests that they answer to something more than convenience.

The traditional defense offers three reasons. The first is evidentiary: memories fade, documents disappear, and witnesses die, so that a trial held long after the events is likelier to reach an erroneous verdict. The second is repose: people should be able to arrange their affairs, sell property, and plan their lives without the lingering threat of an old claim. The third is diligence: a claimant who sleeps on his rights forfeits them, and the prospect of a bar encourages those who have been wronged to act while the facts are fresh. Each reason has force, but each also has an obvious limit. Evidence may be preserved in recordings and in laboratories, so a rule keyed to the calendar is both too rough and too crude a proxy for the quality of the proof. And the diligence rationale presumes that the claimant could have acted earlier, which is not always so.

The exceptions to the rule are instructive. Most jurisdictions place no time limit on prosecutions for murder, and many have extended or suspended the period for crimes against children, on the ground that a child victim may not understand, or be able to report, what was done for many years. The law of civil claims has developed a discovery rule under which the clock does not begin to run until the injured person knew, or reasonably should have known, of the harm; a patient who learns of a surgical instrument left inside her body decades later is not treated as having slept on her rights. Some legislatures have gone further and opened temporary windows during which claims otherwise barred may be filed. These revival laws are controversial. Critics say they upset settled expectations, since defendants who were entitled to consider the matter closed are suddenly exposed, and that the loss of evidence may make a fair defense impossible. Supporters respond that the very harm alleged may be the reason for the delay, since many victims of abuse are silenced by shame, fear, or dependence on the wrongdoer.

These disputes suggest that the best way to understand limitation periods is not as a verdict that old wrongs do not matter, nor as a mere convenience, but as a way of allocating the risk of uncertainty. Every legal system has to decide who will bear the cost of not knowing what happened long ago, and a fixed deadline places that cost on the claimant who could have acted and did not. The justification collapses in those cases where the delay is attributable to the wrong itself, because a rule that rewards the wrongdoer for the success of his concealment or the severity of his victim's injury turns the protection of repose into a reward for the offense. What looks like a conflict between justice and convenience is therefore better seen as a difficulty in deciding whose silence the law should treat as a choice.

questions.stem: Which of the following best states the main idea of the passage?

options.A: Limitation periods are best understood as a way of allocating the risk of uncertainty, with exceptions where the delay results from the wrong itself.
options.B: Statutes of limitations place administrative convenience above justice and should be abolished for serious wrongs.
options.C: Revival windows are justified because modern recordkeeping has undermined the evidentiary rationale for limitation periods, so old claims can now be tried fairly.
options.D: The diligence rationale is the strongest of the traditional justifications for barring old claims.

questions.explanation: Correct: A) The final paragraph states this directly. Why the others are wrong: B) The author does not call for abolition. C) The author notes evidence may be preserved but does not use this to justify revival. D) The author finds it weak where claimants could not have acted earlier.
questions.trap: Choosing a claim about one rationale instead of the author's overall reinterpretation.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT among the traditional rationales for limitation periods described in the passage?

options.A: Old wrongs become less serious as time passes.
options.B: Evidence deteriorates as memories fade and witnesses die.
options.C: People should be able to plan their affairs free of old claims.
options.D: Claimants should be encouraged to act while the facts are fresh.

questions.explanation: Correct: A) The first paragraph says a wrong does not become less wrong with time; this is not a rationale. Why the others are wrong: B) This is the evidentiary rationale. C) This is the repose rationale. D) This is the diligence rationale.
questions.trap: Missing the word NOT and choosing the first rationale that matches the passage.

questions.stem: The author describes the patient who discovers a retained surgical instrument decades later in order to illustrate:

options.A: the discovery rule, under which the period begins when the harm is or should be known.
options.B: a revival window opened by a legislature for claims that are otherwise barred by the ordinary deadline.
options.C: the absence of any time limit on prosecutions for the gravest crimes.
options.D: the repose rationale as applied to medical professionals.

questions.explanation: Correct: A) The passage introduces the example with the discovery rule. Why the others are wrong: B) Revival windows are described separately. C) This is the murder example. D) The example favors the claimant, not repose.
questions.trap: Connecting the example to the wrong exception among several described in the same paragraph.

questions.stem: The author says the diligence rationale "presumes that the claimant could have acted earlier" in order to:

options.A: argue that claimants who delay deserve no protection from the courts.
options.B: show that the rationale fails where the claimant had no real opportunity to sue.
options.C: suggest that preserved evidence makes diligence unnecessary in modern cases.
options.D: establish that most claimants delay deliberately in order to gain a tactical edge.

questions.explanation: Correct: B) The author notes this presumption is not always true. Why the others are wrong: A) This is the rationale the author is limiting. C) This is the point of the preceding sentence about the evidentiary rationale. D) The author makes no claim about deliberate delay.
questions.trap: Confusing the author's point about diligence with the earlier point about evidence.

questions.stem: Which of the following would the author's final argument most likely treat as justifying suspension of a limitation period?

options.A: A plaintiff delays suing for years because she is occupied with her career.
options.B: A claimant forgets that a debt was owed to her until after the period expires.
options.C: A defendant moves to a distant city after the deadline and becomes hard to locate.
options.D: An employer conceals records of a safety defect until after the usual period expires.

questions.explanation: Correct: D) Here the delay is caused by the wrongdoer's concealment. Why the others are wrong: A) This is delay the claimant could have avoided. B) Forgetting is the claimant's own lapse. C) The wrong did not cause the delay, and the move comes after the deadline.
questions.trap: Choosing a sympathetic delay not caused by the wrong itself.

questions.stem: Which of the following findings would most strengthen the critics' objection to revival laws?

options.A: Many claimants in revived cases said fear of the wrongdoer was the reason for their delay.
options.B: Revival windows led to a large increase in the number of claims filed.
options.C: Defendants in revived cases were frequently unable to present evidence that had existed when the claims arose.
options.D: Legislatures that opened revival windows later lengthened the ordinary limitation periods.

questions.explanation: Correct: C) This supports the concern that a fair defense becomes impossible. Why the others are wrong: A) This supports the supporters. B) Volume alone does not show unfairness. D) This does not bear on fairness to defendants.
questions.trap: Choosing evidence that favors the supporters or that is irrelevant to the critics' specific concern.

passages.passage_text:
The lecture has been declared obsolete so often that its survival requires explanation. In the medieval university, where the practice took shape, the explanation was obvious: books were copied by hand, and a manuscript of a major text was worth the price of a farm. A master read the text aloud, the students copied it down, and the master added glosses. The very word lecture derives from the Latin for reading. The invention of printing removed the original reason, since a student who could buy the book no longer needed to hear it recited, and critics from the sixteenth century onward have asked why professors continued to read aloud what the students could read for themselves.

The modern criticism is usually phrased in the language of learning science. Students listening to a lecture are passive, the critics say, and passivity is the enemy of understanding. Experiments in which classes are randomly assigned to lecture or to active formats, such as small-group problem solving, tend to find that students in the latter do better on examinations and are less likely to fail. Some universities have responded by replacing lecture halls with studios in which students work in teams, and a few have flatly urged the abolition of the lecture. Defenders usually reply by pointing to the brilliance of the great lecturers or by appealing to tradition, and neither answer is satisfying.

The strongest defense begins by questioning what the critics assume a lecture is for. If its purpose is to transmit information, then printing, and now the internet, made it redundant, and the experiments show that other methods transmit information more efficiently. But a good lecture does something different. It lets students watch an expert think in real time: choosing an approach, hitting a difficulty, backing up, and recovering. A textbook presents the finished argument, polished to hide its false starts, and a student who reads only textbooks may conclude that understanding arrives without effort and in a straight line. A lecture can model the stumbling by which understanding is actually reached, and it can respond to the audience's expressions of confusion, adjusting its pace and its examples as it goes. The argument is therefore that the lecture's value lies in a skill, reasoning in public, that examinations of recall do not measure.

This reply has weaknesses, and its proponents should concede them. The great majority of lectures do not show anyone thinking; they present notes that have not changed in a decade, and in that case the critics are right that a recording would serve as well. The comparisons that favor active formats are also not simply the artifacts of bad measurement, since many of them do assess problem solving as well as recall. Still, the defense shifts the burden of proof in a useful way. It shows that comparing the lecture with its alternatives on a single outcome tells us little until we say which outcome the form exists to produce. The right conclusion is neither that the lecture is obsolete nor that it is sacred, but that its worth depends on whether the person at the lectern is using it for the one thing it can still do better than print.

questions.stem: Which of the following best expresses the main argument of the passage?

options.A: The lecture is obsolete because print and the internet transmit information more efficiently than a speaker can, so students should simply read the material themselves.
options.B: The worth of the lecture depends on whether it is used to model expert reasoning, which print cannot do, rather than to transmit information.
options.C: Active-learning experiments show that lecturing is a poor method that should be replaced by studio formats.
options.D: The lecture persists because of tradition and the brilliance of its best practitioners.

questions.explanation: Correct: B) The fourth paragraph says the lecture's worth depends on the outcome the form exists to produce. Why the others are wrong: A) The author says this is true only if transmitting information is its purpose. C) The author says the defense shifts the burden of proof. D) The author calls those defenses unsatisfying.
questions.trap: Choosing the position of one side of the dispute rather than the author's qualified conclusion.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the original reason for the lecture was:

options.A: the belief that students learn better from hearing a text than from reading it.
options.B: the scarcity and cost of handwritten books.
options.C: the need for masters to add commentary that no manuscript could contain.
options.D: the expectation that students would answer the master's questions during the reading.

questions.explanation: Correct: B) Manuscripts were costly, so a master read the text aloud. Why the others are wrong: A) The passage gives no such belief. C) Glosses were added but the reason for reading aloud was scarcity. D) Student questions are not mentioned.
questions.trap: Choosing a pedagogical motive when the passage gives a material one.

questions.stem: The author finds the defenders' appeals to great lecturers and to tradition unsatisfying because:

options.A: both concede that most lectures are rarely brilliant.
options.B: both assume the lecture is more valuable than student success, however much students may learn elsewhere.
options.C: neither is supported by any experimental evidence at all.
options.D: neither answers the charge that lectures promote learning less well than other methods.

questions.explanation: Correct: D) The author calls the replies unsatisfying after describing the experimental criticism. Why the others are wrong: A) No such concession is made. B) This is not stated. C) The author does not make this claim.
questions.trap: Reading a general complaint about relevance as a complaint about evidence.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a limitation of the author's defense that the passage itself acknowledges?

options.A: Textbooks present arguments in a way that conceals the false starts of discovery, which is why students need lectures.
options.B: Most lectures do not display reasoning in progress, so a recording would serve as well.
options.C: Experiments favoring active formats measure only recall and not problem solving.
options.D: Lectures cannot respond to students' confusion in real time.

questions.explanation: Correct: B) The final paragraph concedes this. Why the others are wrong: A) This is part of the defense. C) The author says many of them assess problem solving too. D) The author claims lectures can respond to confusion.
questions.trap: Choosing a statement drawn from the defense instead of the concessions.

questions.stem: Which of the following findings would most strengthen the author's claim about what a good lecture does?

options.A: Students who attended lectures scored higher on recall tests than students who read the textbook.
options.B: Students who watched an expert solve unfamiliar problems aloud later solved new problems better than students given only the finished solutions.
options.C: Students in team-based studios reported greater satisfaction than students in lecture halls.
options.D: Lecturers who reused identical notes for a decade received strong ratings from students.

questions.explanation: Correct: B) This supports the value of watching reasoning in progress. Why the others are wrong: A) This concerns recall, not the modeling of reasoning. C) This concerns satisfaction in the competing format. D) This does not show the effect of modeled reasoning.
questions.trap: Choosing evidence about recall or satisfaction when the claim concerns modeling reasoning.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the best analogy for the author's argument about the lecture?

options.A: Watching a chef teaches recovery from mistakes in a way recipe books cannot.
options.B: A detailed map has been replaced by satellite navigation because both give directions to the same destination.
options.C: A professional sports league uses videos of past games to attract spectators who cannot attend in person.
options.D: A bank uses an automated teller for routine transactions to reduce the time spent with staff.

questions.explanation: Correct: A) Both defend a live demonstration of process that a finished text conceals. Why the others are wrong: B) This resembles the transmission view the author rejects. C) This is about broadcasting rather than showing process. D) This is about efficiency, not about showing how skill works.
questions.trap: Choosing an analogy about efficient delivery of the same product.

passages.passage_text:
Few moral ideas are praised as warmly as forgiveness, and few are as poorly understood. Religious traditions commend it, therapists recommend it, and popular wisdom promises that the one who forgives will be freed from the burden of bitterness. The very warmth of this consensus conceals several quarrels. Is forgiveness something that wronged persons owe? Does it require the wrongdoer to repent? And what exactly is being given up when someone forgives?

To answer the last question, it helps to say what forgiveness is not. It is not excusing, which holds that the wrongdoer was not responsible, and it is not condoning, which treats the wrong as acceptable. A person who forgives a betrayal still regards it as a betrayal; that is why there is something to forgive. Nor is forgiveness the same as reconciliation, which restores a relationship and requires the other party's cooperation. A woman may forgive the man who injured her and decline ever to see him again. What forgiveness gives up, on the most plausible account, is a particular set of responses to the wrong: resentment, the wish to see the wrongdoer suffer, and the settled tendency to treat him as defined by what he did.

Philosophers in the tradition of Bishop Butler have pointed out that resentment is not merely a painful feeling. It is a form of moral protest, an expression of the conviction that one deserved better and that the wrong mattered. A person who feels no resentment at being abused may be showing not generosity but a lack of self-respect. This observation explains why forgiveness cannot be demanded. If the wronged person owed forgiveness, then withholding it would be a fault, and many victims would be doubly burdened: first by the injury, then by the charge that they were failing to move on. Insisting that victims forgive, particularly when the wrongdoer shows no regret, risks turning a gift into a debt and allowing the offender to collect on it.

At the same time, forgiveness is not arbitrary, and it is not only a matter of private feeling. Most of us believe that forgiveness is more fitting when the wrongdoer has acknowledged the wrong, apologized, and tried to repair the damage, since these acts change what he is saying about the victim: where the offense implied that she did not count, the apology says that she does. Without such acts, forgiving may look like a kind of surrender. Yet this raises a puzzle about the cases of people who forgive unrepentant wrongdoers, sometimes publicly and in spite of every provocation, and are admired for it. One response is that such people are doing something different, which might better be called letting go: refusing to let the offender's act continue to organize their own lives. That is a real good, and it is within the power of the victim alone. But it is not the same good as forgiveness proper, which is addressed to the wrongdoer and answers to something he has done. Keeping the two apart lets us honor the generosity of the one without pretending that the other has been owed or earned.

questions.stem: Which of the following best summarizes the author's position?

options.A: Forgiveness cannot be owed and is most fitting after repentance, though a victim may separately let go of the wrong without forgiving.
options.B: Forgiveness is a duty of the wronged, since resentment harms those who keep it.
options.C: Forgiveness and reconciliation are identical, since both restore the relationship between wrongdoer and victim and require both parties to take part.
options.D: Unrepentant wrongdoers should be forgiven, since forgiveness depends only on the victim's feelings.

questions.explanation: Correct: A) The passage argues that forgiveness cannot be demanded, fits repentance, and differs from letting go. Why the others are wrong: B) The author says forgiveness cannot be demanded. C) The author distinguishes them. D) The author says forgiveness answers to what the wrongdoer has done.
questions.trap: Choosing the popular view the passage begins by questioning.

questions.stem: According to the passage, resentment is:

options.A: a painful feeling that forgiveness is meant to eliminate in every case.
options.B: an emotion indicating that the wrongdoer ought to be punished in some way.
options.C: a form of moral protest that may reflect self-respect.
options.D: a reaction that is excusable in victims who have been unable to move on from an injury.

questions.explanation: Correct: C) The third paragraph describes it this way. Why the others are wrong: A) The author says feeling none at abuse may reflect a lack of self-respect. B) The wish to see the wrongdoer suffer is one response forgiveness gives up, but this is not the passage's account. D) The author does not treat resentment as an excuse.
questions.trap: Seeing resentment only as a harmful feeling to be overcome.

questions.stem: The author argues that forgiveness cannot be demanded because:

options.A: it would require victims to excuse wrongs that were not wrong.
options.B: it would imply that the offender need not apologize.
options.C: it would conflict with the rule that reconciliation requires mutual agreement.
options.D: demanding it would burden victims a second time and let offenders collect on a gift as though it were a debt.

questions.explanation: Correct: D) The third paragraph states this. Why the others are wrong: A) Excusing is a different concept the author distinguishes. B) The author says nothing of this kind. C) Reconciliation is distinguished from forgiveness.
questions.trap: Importing the distinction among excusing, condoning, and forgiving into the demand argument.

questions.stem: A woman publicly forgives a man who has shown no remorse for injuring her. The author would most likely say that she:

options.A: has failed to show self-respect, since resentment was the only fitting response to a man who showed no remorse.
options.B: has excused the man by denying that his act was wrong.
options.C: has done something admirable that is better described as letting go than as forgiveness proper.
options.D: has reconciled with the man, since forgiveness requires restoring the relationship.

questions.explanation: Correct: C) The final paragraph proposes this description of such cases. Why the others are wrong: A) The author says forgiving unrepentant wrongdoers can be admirable. B) Forgiveness does not deny the wrong. D) The author separates forgiveness from reconciliation.
questions.trap: Reading admiration for the act as agreement that it is forgiveness proper.

questions.stem: Which of the following findings would most challenge the author's claim that apology makes forgiveness more fitting?

options.A: Most people judge forgiveness of unrepentant wrongdoers to be more fitting than forgiveness of repentant ones.
options.B: Most people judge that victims should not be required to forgive wrongdoers who are remorseful, since forgiveness is a gift.
options.C: Wrongdoers who apologize are more likely to be reconciled with their victims than those who do not.
options.D: Victims who forgive unrepentant wrongdoers report feeling less bitterness than victims who do not.

questions.explanation: Correct: A) This would contradict the intuition on which the claim rests. Why the others are wrong: B) This agrees with the argument that forgiveness is not owed. C) This concerns reconciliation, not fittingness. D) This concerns benefit to victims, which the author separates from fittingness.
questions.trap: Choosing a finding about outcomes when the claim concerns what is fitting.
